Significant International Environmental 
Law Developments: 2022–2023
James Harrison*
1.  INTRODUCTION
The seriousness of the environmental crises we face are becoming increasingly clear as each year 
passes. Temperatures are rising, with predictions that the global average temperature is likely to 
exceed 1.5°C in the next five years.1 Climate change also compounds existing pressures that we 
place on the natural environment, leading to additional threats to biodiversity. The situation will 
only get worse unless transformational change takes place. In this context, a critical question is 
whether international law is sufficiently nimble to affect such change in time.
This is one of the questions that has been recently considered by the High-Level Advisory 
Board on Effective Multilateralism (HLABEM), established by the UN Secretary-General to 
develop concrete proposals to advance the themes addressed in the Our Common Agenda Report 
published in 2021.2 The outcome of this process is a report titled ‘A Breakthrough for People 
and Planet’ which calls for ‘a less hierarchical, more networked system wherein decision-making 
is distributed, and where the efforts of a large number of different actors are harnessed towards 
a collective mission’.3 There is an emphasis on inclusiveness and particularly gender equality, 
which is mirrored in other developments discussed below.4 The report identifies six necessary 
‘shifts’ that must take place, including ‘deliver[ing] for people and planet by regaining balance 
with nature and providing clean energy for all’.5 The specific proposals under this title include 
the conclusion of a pact for people and planet, reform of the global trade, investment and intel-
lectual property system, and a stronger role for the United Nations Environment Programme in 
the intergovernmental system.6 The report also emphasises the need for appropriate account-
ability mechanisms ‘that [hold] all actors responsible and generates behavioural change at the

global level’.7 These proposals should be read alongside the more general recommendations for 
strengthening the multilateral system with an emphasis on greater participation, particularly of 
women, youth and indigenous groups, and more effective decision-making through a move-
ment towards ‘qualified majority, double majority or non-unanimous definitions of consensus 
voting systems’.8
Of course, these are not the first calls for radical reform of the international system. In his 1992 
essay on international environmental law-making, Sir Geoffrey Palmer argued that nations need 
to surrender some sovereignty in order to achieve more effective international environmental 
governance and in this light, he suggested the establishment of an International Environmental 
Organisation modelled on the International Labour Organisation.9 More recently, proposals 
for a global pact on the environment included a draft text for a new instrument that has not yet 
gained much traction with states.10 It remains to be seen how palatable this newly presented 
recipe for change will be to states, who will have to decide whether they are willing to concede 
control over international law-making in favour of a more effective and equitable global order.
In the meantime, international environmental law continues to develop at a slow pace. 
Nevertheless, 2022–23 has seen some notable breakthroughs in diplomatic negotiations in the 
environmental field. The following sections will provide a summary of several significant devel-
opments in international environmental law between May 2022 and July 2023, with a particular 
focus on biodiversity, climate change and environmental rights. There has been more limited 
international case law on environmental matters in the past year, but the survey highlights sev-
eral eagerly awaited judicial decisions that are expected in the year to come.
2.  BIODIVERITY BREAKTHROUGHS
The global biodiversity regime often stands in the shadow of its more prominent sibling, the cli-
mate change regime. However, major developments in the biodiversity regime hit the headlines 
twice in 2022–23.
Firstly, the fifteenth Conference of the Parties (COP) to the Convention on Biological 
Diversity (CBD)11 adopted its new strategic plan for the period 2022–2030.12 The so-called 
Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF) seeks to deliver progress towards 
the overarching vision of the Convention, namely ‘by 2050, biodiversity is valued, conserved, 
restored and wisely used, maintaining ecosystem services, sustaining a healthy planet and 
delivering benefits essential for all people’.13 To achieve this vision, transformational change is 
required, particularly as the current trend is towards continuing biodiversity loss. Indeed, the 
last strategic plan can only be considered a failure, as the vast majority of targets were either not 
met or only partially met.14 It is therefore no surprise that the new GBF emphasises the need for 
urgent action across the whole of society to reverse biodiversity loss and restore ecosystems.15 
The GBF is structured around four long-term goals relating to the 2050 vision accompanied

469
by ‘23 action-orientated global targets for urgent action over the decade to 2030’.16 Particular 
highlights include:
•	 Ensure that at least 30% of degraded ecosystems are under effective restoration (target 2)
•	 Ensure that at least 30% of terrestrial, inland water and coastal and marine areas are effec-
tively conserved and managed through systems of protected areas (target 3)
•	 Ensure action to halt human induced extinction of known threatened species (target 4)
•	 Reduce pollution risks from all sources to levels that are not harmful to biodiversity and 
ecosystem functions and services, with a particular focus on excess nutrients, pesticides 
and highly hazardous chemicals (target 7)
Alongside these specific biodiversity targets, the GBF also establishes a clear value system for 
implementation of the framework, including an emphasis on a human-rights based approach17 
and, echoing the report of the HLABEM, ‘gender equality and empowerment of women and 
girls’.18
CBD Parties are expected to revise their national biodiversity strategies to align with the new 
targets and the GBF explicitly recognises that achievement of the goals will depend upon the 
provision of ‘adequate, predictable and easily accessible financial resources’.19 Implementation 
of the GBF will be overseen through a reporting procedure and a ‘global review of collective 
progress’ to take place at COP 17 and COP 19.20 This process would seem to be modelled on 
the ‘global stocktake’ under the Paris Agreement,21 adapted to a biodiversity context, and it is 
emphasised that it will take place in a ‘facilitative, non-intrusive, non-punitive manner, respect-
ing national sovereignty, and avoiding placing undue burden on Parties, in particular developing 
countries’.22 Indeed, it must be remembered that the GBF is only a decision of the CBD COP 
and it does not establish legally binding commitments for states. At the same time, there is a 
legal instrument which underpins the GBF and, despite its notably open-textured language, it 
can be asked whether more could be done to hold states to account on the legal plane for their 
compliance with the CBD.
The second major breakthrough for global biodiversity conservation was the conclusion of 
a new legally binding Agreement under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea 
on the conservation and sustainable use of marine biological diversity of areas beyond national 
jurisdiction, colloquially referred to as the ‘BBNJ Agreement’.23 The treaty was formally adopted 
on 19 June 2023, following a long and difficult negotiation process. Indeed, the fact that states 
were able to agree on the text at all is something to be celebrated, particularly in the current 
geopolitical atmosphere. The Agreement is designed to address perceived gaps in coverage or 
implementation of the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS),24 
with a focus on developing the ocean governance framework for those areas beyond national 
jurisdiction, namely the high seas and the International Seabed Area.

James Harrison
The BBNJ Agreement covers four main substantive issues, namely marine genetic resources 
(MGRs), area-based management tools, environmental impact assessment (EIA), and technol-
ogy transfer and capacity building. The complexity and sensitivity of many of these issues meant 
that compromises were necessary in order to achieve agreement and many of the provisions 
fall short of what some had hoped for when the process first started more than a decade ago. 
Nevertheless, the Agreement will introduce a new pillar in the global ocean governance archi-
tecture and therefore it is important to understand what it entails.
On EIA, the Agreement reiterates the requirement in Article 206 of UNCLOS to carry out an 
environmental assessment of activities which may cause ‘substantial pollution of or significant 
and harmful changes to the marine environment’25 with the addition of a number of procedural 
steps that must be taken, including a screening exercise and requirements to notify and consult 
not only other states, but also indigenous peoples, local communities, relevant global, regional 
and subregional and sectoral bodies, civil society, the scientific community and the public at 
large.26 The broad range of stakeholders to be consulted under the Agreement reinforces that 
areas beyond national jurisdiction are to be treated as a global commons in which we all have an 
interest. In addition, the Agreement establishes a bespoke Scientific and Technical Body to inter 
alia make comments on draft environmental impact assessment reports.27 The Agreement is one 
of the first international instruments in which ‘gender balance’ is explicitly included as a consid-
eration in the composition of treaty bodies, alongside the traditional geographical representa-
tion.28 Whilst a wide range of actors can have a say on a proposed activity, the BBNJ Agreement 
confirms that it is the party under whose jurisdiction or control a planned activity falls who 
shall be responsible for determining if it may proceed, and for monitoring and reviewing the 
impacts of authorised activities.29 In other words, flag state jurisdiction remains a key principle 
of the new agreement, despite calls during the negotiations for greater international control over 
activities in areas beyond national jurisdiction.
Similar procedural mechanisms are applied to proposals to establish area-based management 
measures in areas beyond national jurisdiction.30 In this case, a proposal may be adopted by the 
COP to the Agreement, which is empowered to take ‘decisions on the establishment of area-
based management tools, including marine protected areas, and related measures’.31 A key issue 
in the negotiations was the interrelationship between the COP and existing intergovernmental 
organisations and processes. According to the final text, ‘in taking decisions [on area-based man-
agement tools], the [COP] shall respect the competences of, and not undermine, relevant legal 
instruments and frameworks and relevant global, regional, subregional and sectoral bodies’.32 
Indeed, there is a requirement for decisions on measures to be ‘compatible with those adopted 
by relevant legal instruments and frameworks and relevant global, regional and subregional and 
sectoral bodies’33 and where a measure is within the competence of another instrument, body 
or framework, the COP can make recommendations, rather than taking the decision itself.34 
The key ingredient for the success of this mechanism will therefore be cooperation between the 
COP and other relevant instruments, bodies and frameworks35 and it is envisaged that the COP

471
may in some circumstances play a coordinating role amongst existing bodies.36 The powers of 
the COP to adopt conservation measures in areas beyond national jurisdiction are also subject 
to a complex decision-making formula. The Agreement, whilst encouraging consensus, ulti-
mately rests upon traditional consent-based decision-making, requiring a three-fourths major-
ity of parties present and voting to support a decision.37 The Agreement also allows individual 
parties to opt-out of decisions adopted by the COP provided that they give an explanation and 
they adopt, to the extent practicable, alternative measures or approaches that are equivalent 
in effect to the decision to which they have objected.38 This provides some safeguards against 
abuse, although much will rely upon how the conditions attached to the power to object are 
interpreted and how they are enforced in practice.
Whilst EIA and area-based management tools were to some extent covered, albeit imper-
fectly, by existing law, UNCLOS contained a clear lacuna when it came to MGRs. This was per-
haps one of the most controversial issues during the negotiations as it involved a debate about 
whether MGRs should be subject to freedom of scientific research or whether their use should 
be the common heritage of humankind. The final agreement adopts a compromise position, 
with both principles acknowledged in the general principles of the Agreement39 and Part II on 
MGRs steering a tight course between the two. The objective of Part II is ‘the fair and equitable 
sharing of benefits arising from activities with respect to [MGRs] and digital sequence infor-
mation on [MGRs] of areas beyond national jurisdiction’, as well as building the capacity of 
developing countries to participate in such activities.40 The Agreement does not restrict who 
can access MGRs, recognising that all states may do so.41 At the same time, it requires signifi-
cant transparency about proposed activities and the outcomes of these activities.42 A number of 
other obligations concerning the fair and equitable sharing of benefits apply to activities con-
nected with MGRs collected from areas beyond national jurisdiction. Firstly, certain non-mon-
etary benefits must be shared, including access to samples and digital sequence information 
‘in accordance with current international practice’.43 This means that the entity collecting the 
resource cannot monopolise the study of the resource. Of course, individual persons or entities 
may still develop commercial applications based upon MGRs which may be subject to exclusive 
intellectual property rights. Whilst explicit language on the relationship between the Agreement 
and intellectual property law was eventually removed from the Agreement, it still makes clear 
that patents can be granted, provided that they are notified to the Clearing House Mechanism 
established under the Agreement.44 Nevertheless, the holder of a patent may be under an obli-
gation to share monetary benefits from the utilisation of MGRs, such as milestone payments or 
royalties, under a scheme to be agreed by the COP.45 The full effects of this new framework are 
therefore still to be worked out in future negotiations. Moreover, further work may be needed 
on the relationship of the new arrangements with the international intellectual property regime 
and it is worth noting that the World Intellectual Property Organisation (WIPO) is already 
hosting negotiations on an international legal instrument on intellectual property issues related 
to genetic resources, intended to prevent the granting of erroneous patents and to ensure

compliance with access and benefit-sharing arrangements, such as the one that will be estab-
lished under the BBNJ Agreement.46
The final element of the BBNJ Agreement relates to capacity building and technology trans-
fer. This is already a topic that is dealt with in depth by UNCLOS,47 although implementation 
has fallen short of expectations. The BBNJ Agreement does little to impose substantive new 
obligations, but rather emphasises the modalities for capacity building and technology trans-
fer,48 particularly emphasising the need for capacity building to be country-driven and respon-
sive to the needs of the recipient state. Moreover, it establishes a new institutional framework, 
including a specialist committee,49 which will be responsible for monitoring and reviewing pro-
gress towards the objectives set by this Part of the Agreement.50
The BBNJ Agreement has been widely welcomed, but, in order to have its desired effect, it 
must first enter into force. Sixty parties must ratify the Agreement in order for this to happen,51 
although the Agreement can arguably only be truly successful if it achieves quasi-universal par-
ticipation, given that all states have a right to carry out activities on the high seas.52 Political 
effort to support ratification will therefore be vital in the short-term.53 Furthermore, although 
the treaty negotiations have now concluded, there is still a lot of work to do in order to give 
effect to these provisions through the adoption of further modalities and procedures. Some 
difficult issues remain on the table, particularly in the context of MGRs and operationalising the 
provisions on monetary benefit-sharing. In terms of how far the Agreement will contribute to 
reducing biodiversity loss, the real effectiveness of the Agreement will depend in large part upon 
how the new tools and procedures will be utilised and whether agreement can be reached on 
ambitious measures to protect and preserve, as well as to enhance and restore, marine ecosys-
tems in some of the more remote parts of the planet. In this connection, the BBNJ Agreement 
must also be read alongside the GBF and the latter instrument should be used as a guiding star 
for the implementation of the Agreement.
3.  CHAMPIONING CLIMATE CHANGE?
With its annual COP, the international climate change regime follows a well-established rou-
tine. In 2022, it was Egypt’s turn to host the 27th COP. Much of the language of the resulting 
Sharm el-Sheikh Implementation Plan54 is familiar to climate documents produced in recent 
years: reiteration of the fact that impacts of climate change will be much lower at a tempera-
ture increase of 1.5°C compared with 2°C;55 recognition that limiting global warming to 1.5°C 
requires ‘rapid, deep and sustained reductions in global greenhouse gas emissions’;56 and urg-
ing states to adopt more ambitious measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, including 
non-carbon dioxide emissions by 2030.57 These pronouncements come only a year before the

473
first formal global stocktake under Article 14 of the Paris Agreement, which is due to take place 
in 2023. Various initiatives to scale up ambition and action were agreed during the Conference, 
including a ‘climate ambition summit’ to be organised by the UN Secretary-General in 2023 and 
the Sharm el-Sheikh mitigation ambition and implementation work programme.58 We will have 
to see whether these initiatives deliver real progress, although, as many reports are increasingly 
highlighting, the time for effective measures to mitigate climate change is running out. This 
is reflected in the COP documentation itself which refers to ‘accelerated action in this critical 
decade’.59 The Sharm el-Sheikh Implementation Plan also underlines that ‘enhanced effective 
climate action should be implemented in a manner that is just and inclusive’,60 which is another 
example of the increasing prominence given to inclusivity and equitable governance at the inter-
national level.61
A major breakthrough of the 27th COP was the adoption of an agreement to establish a 
new loss and damage fund for ‘assisting developing countries that are particularly vulnerable 
to the adverse effects of climate change in responding to loss and damage’.62 However, the COP 
decision does not establish a fully functioning funding arrangement, but rather establishes a 
‘Transitional Committee’ to make recommendations about the modalities to operationalise the 
fund. Nevertheless, it takes a step beyond the text of the Paris Agreement, which addresses loss 
and damage in Article 8, but is silent on funding arrangements. Indeed, lack of funding in the 
climate regime generally remains an issue, with the COP reiterating its call for developed coun-
tries to meet their commitment to mobilise USD 100 billion per year to address the needs of 
developing countries within the climate change regime.63
The UN Framework Convention on Climate Change64 may be the main forum for agreeing 
action on climate change at the global level, but many other treaty regimes also find themselves 
having to address climate change as part of their broader mandate. Greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions from international shipping has been on the agenda of the International Maritime 
Organisation (IMO) for a number of years and July 2023 saw the adoption of a revised IMO 
Strategy on Reduction of GHG Emissions from Ships,65 which is intended to be the IMO’s con-
tribution to meeting the temperature goal under the Paris Agreement.66 The overall ambition 
of the Strategy is to ‘reduc[e] GHG emissions from international shipping and, as a matter of 
urgency, aims to phase them out as soon as possible, while promoting…a just and equitable 
transition’.67 The ultimate goal of the Strategy is reaching net-zero emissions ‘by or around, i.e. 
close to, 2050’, which leaves some wriggle room for states, but the Strategy also sets a (slightly) 
more concrete target of reducing ‘the total annual GHG emissions from international shipping 
by at least 20%, striving for 30%, by 2030, compared to 2008’, and to further reduce this total 
by 70–80% by 2040.68 This is a major step on from the previous interim strategy which had 
only set an indicative target of reducing total GHG emissions from international shipping by

James Harrison
at least 50% by 2050.69 The new IMO targets are to be achieved through a mixture of technical 
measures and economic measures. Short-term technical measures have been put in place70 and 
the Strategy sets a target of 2025 to agree on ‘a basket of mid-term GHG reduction measures’.71 
Thus, further negotiations still lie ahead and the Strategy makes clear that a number of factors, 
beyond climate mitigation, need to be taken into account, including safety aspects associated 
with reducing GHG emissions72 and impacts on states, particularly Least Developed Countries 
and Small Island Developing States, who may rely upon international shipping for the supply of 
essential goods and services.73 A major focus of subsequent work will be on the design and oper-
ation of ships whilst at sea, although the Strategy also notes that gains can be achieved through 
port developments which facilitate access to renewable power supplies.74
Concerns about progress on climate change have also meant that other international regimes 
are being invoked in order to encourage states to take action to meet the global temperature 
targets. Human rights litigation has been a key illustration of this trend that has been discussed 
in previous annual summaries of significant developments in international environmental law.75 
Yet, we are now seeing a broader range of international courts and tribunals brought into the pic-
ture. On top of the request for an advisory opinion from the International Tribunal for the Law 
of the Sea (ITLOS) submitted by a coalition of Small Island Developing States in December 
2022,76 further requests for advisory opinions were made in early 2023 to both the International 
Court of Justice (ICJ)77 and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights (IACHR).78 Whilst 
the requests to ITLOS and the IACHR are concerned with the interpretation and application 
of specific treaties, the request to the ICJ is framed generally, asking in the first question about 
‘the obligations of states under international law to ensure the protection of the climate sys-
tem and other parts of the environment from anthropogenic emissions of greenhouse gases 
for States and for present and future generations’, whilst going on to mention several particular 
treaties: the Charter of the United Nations, the International Covenant on Civil and Political 
Rights, the International Covenant on Economic, Social and Cultural Rights, the United 
Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the Paris Agreement, the United Nations 
Convention on the Law of the Sea—as well as more general rules of customary international 
law.79 As a result, there is potentially an overlap between this request and the requests pending 
before the other courts and tribunals, which raises questions about how, if at all, these judicial 
bodies may coordinate their responses. There are also questions about how specific the answers 
will be, given the broad range of circumstances that they need to address. Yet, the results of these 
requests will only be effective if they can help to move along the climate change debate and pro-
mote further ambitious action by states to address the climate crisis.

4.  HUMAN RIGHTS AND THE ENVIRONMENT
As well as turning their attention to climate change, international human rights courts are also 
familiar with addressing other forms of environmental pollution. Two recent examples are found 
in cases brought against Russia before the European Court of Human Rights. In both cases, the 
Court confirms its established jurisprudence, whilst highlighting the nuances and complexities 
that can arise when applying this case law to the facts of individual cases.
Kotov and others v Russia80 involved a challenge by fourteen residents of the town of Klin 
against the failure of the Russian authorities to effectively regulate a waste management facility 
at Aleksinskiy quarry, run by a private company pursuant to a lease agreement with the Klin 
municipal administration. In particular, the residents complained of foul odours emanating from 
the quarry and they alleged that the waste management facility was being operated in violation 
of applicable environmental regulations. Pavlov and others v Russia81 concerned a challenge by 
residents of Lipetsk against a failure to regulate a number of major industrial undertakings in the 
city, including steelworks, a cement plant and a tractor factory. They also claimed that the oper-
ations had been carried out in violation of domestic environmental standards. Both cases raised 
a number of similar issues concerning the precise scope of protection afforded by the European 
Convention on Human Rights (ECHR)82 to cases of environmental pollution.
The first issue to tax the Court in both cases was the requirement to exhaust available local 
remedies before bringing a claim to the international level. In Kotov, domestic proceedings had 
been initiated by the applicants, but were unsuccessful, with the Klin Town Court rejecting 
the claims. Yet, only the first applicant, Mr Kotov, had pursued appeals against the judgment of 
the local court. As a result, the claims of all applicants, but Mr Kotov, were rejected.83 A similar 
situation pertained in Pavlov, with only 7 out of the 22 applicants having appealed against the 
judgment of the District court. However, in this case, the Court held that ‘the fifteen applicants 
in question were absolved from the obligation to exhaust domestic remedies because they were 
in a very similar situation as the other seven applicants who brought the appeal and they were 
affected in the same way by those proceedings’.84 What seems to separate the cases is that the 
affected applicants in Kotov had either not instigated proceedings at all or had abandoned pro-
ceedings without justification.85 In contrast, in Pavlov, the Court seems to accept that there was 
a justification for only some of the applicants pursuing further remedies given their similarity of 
situation, although their reasoning on this point is vague. Indeed, Judge Lobov dissented from 
the decision in Pavlov, on the basis that no satisfactory explanation or justification had been 
given and explaining that, in their view, ‘allowing the applicants to proceed is tantamount to giv-
ing carte blanche to any one of the 500,000 inhabitants of the city to join any such application 
without first making a meaningful effort to press domestic courts for solutions’.86
Secondly, the cases raised questions about the threshold of severity that must be met in order 
to bring a successful claim under Article 8 of the ECHR concerning the protection of private 
and family life. A similar position was taken in both cases, where the applicants had not asserted 
any particular medical evidence of harm, but rather they complained of being affected by the 
generally poor state of the environment in which they lived. It was therefore impossible for the 
Court to establish a clear causal linked between the activities complained of and the alleged

evidence relating to pollution levels in order to conclude that ‘living in the area marked by pol-
lution in clear excess of the applicable safety standards makes [Mr Kotov] more vulnerable 
to various illnesses’.87 Moreover, the Court underlined that it is not necessary to demonstrate 
impacts on physical health in order to succeed in a claim under Article 8 as ‘severe environmen-
tal pollution may affect individuals’ well-being in such a way as to affect their private and family 
life adversely, without, however, seriously endangering their health’.88 The Court accepted that 
the environmental nuisances of which Mr Kotov complained were not negligible and triggered 
Article 8 of the Convention. A similar approach was taken in Pavlov, but the case raised more 
complex issues because it was not concerned with a single facility but rather a range of polluting 
activities. Moreover, not all of the applicants lived within the immediate vicinity of the pollu-
tion, with several of them living up to 15 km from the operations complained of. Yet, the Court 
emphasised that proximity to pollution is only one of the factors to be taken into account in 
determining whether the threshold of seriousness has been crossed to trigger Article 8.89 In par-
ticular, the Court highlighted evidence that Lipetsk was one of the most polluted cities in Russia 
with all areas of the city registering levels of pollution in excess of applicable safety standards. 
The Court was careful to say that the mere identification of excessive pollution levels may not be 
enough to trigger Article 8 in all cases,90 but the evidence in the case at hand pointed to serious 
risks for the entire population over a significant period of time. The cases therefore demonstrate 
the willingness of the Court to set a flexible evidential threshold in cases concerning environ-
mental pollution.
Thirdly, the Court had to determine whether the state had taken sufficient action to address 
the pollution in each case. Kotov was a simpler case given that it concerned a single facility run 
by one operator. The Court noted that the legal regime for waste management facilities in Russia 
provides for strict regulation, but the Court identified a number of legal requirements which had 
not been enforced by public authorities, despite evidence of non-compliance by the operator.91 
However, the Court also noted that the government had been more active in overseeing the 
operation since 2019. Therefore the finding of a violation of Article 8 was limited to the period 
2015 (when the complaint was made) to 2018. In Pavlov, the Court similarly carried out an 
analysis of what had been done by the public authorities to prevent pollution from the relevant 
facilities in order to assess whether they had ‘approached the problem with due diligence and 
gave consideration to all the competing interests’.92 Like the situation in Kotov, the Court noted 
that there authorities had improved their performance over time by taking increased measures 
to monitor and promote a reduction in pollution. Indeed, the Court recognised the challenges 
of adopting effective measures in a timely manner when there were a number of competing 
interests to reconcile. However, the Court was not convinced that the state had justified the 
delay in action93 and even when measures had been taken, the Court held that ‘industrial air pol-
lution in Lipetsk has not been sufficiently curbed, so as to prevent that the residents of that city 
be exposed to related health risks’.94 The government had therefore failed to meet the require-

afforded a sufficient margin of appreciation to the domestic authorities which faced ‘a delicate 
balancing exercise between, on the one hand, the reduction of industrial pollution, and on the

In both of these cases, Judge Serghides attached a concurring opinion in which they empha-
sised the importance of the continuing evolution of the human rights case law to address 
environmental challenges and they suggested the emergence of a new ‘sub-right to a healthy 
environment’ which should be interpreted broadly, with strict control over any interference 
with the right. In their separate opinion in Pavlov, Judge Krenc also pointed to the need to 
ensure that the ECHR was interpreted in light of broader developments in international law.
One such development, explicitly mentioned by Judge Krenc, was the adoption by the UN 
General Assembly in July 2022 of a resolution ‘recogniz[ing] the right to a clean, healthy and 
sustainable environment as a human right’.97 This instrument represents a further milestone in 
the work on human rights and the environment that has been carried out within the UN system 
in recent years.98 The precise legal implications of this instrument must be treated with caution, 
however. Judge Krenc, in their separate opinion in Pavlov, pointed out that all member states of 
the Council of Europe had voted in favour of the Resolution,99 which, Judge Krenc suggested, 
indicated common ground between the member states that must be taken into account in inter-
preting the ECHR. Yet, the position of many states is more nuanced that it might seem. Thus, 
in their explanation of the vote on the resolution, several states, including Council of Europe 
members, noted that they supported the resolution but they asserted that the right has not yet 
attained the status of customary international law.100 Indeed, it was highlighted in the United 
Nations General Assembly debate on the resolution that there was a need to develop a common 
understanding of what a right might entail.101 In particular, it will be interesting to reflect on how 
a new substantive right may go further than the jurisprudence which has seen the expansion of 
existing rights to an increasing range of environmental matters.

with the decision in the Dispute over the Status and Use of the Waters of the Silala.103 The Silala 
River is a transboundary watercourse that begins in the Bolivian Andes, before flowing into 
Chile where it meets with the San Pedro River. The dispute concerned whether Bolivia had 
complied with relevant rules of customary international law in authorising several proposed 
activities on the Silala River. Bolivia also raised a number of related counter-claims about its 
right to remove certain infrastructure which had been installed in order to enhance the flow of 
the river, although the Court refused to deal with these aspects of the dispute, either because 
they were moot104 or they concerned future hypothetical situations.105
At the outset, the Court confirmed that both parties had a basic right to an equitable and 
reasonable sharing of the resources of the river and a concomitant duty to ‘take all appropriate 
measures to prevent the causing of significant harm to the other Party’.106 These substantive 
duties are accompanied by certain procedural obligations, such as requirements of notification 
and consultation concerning certain activities. A key issue that divided the parties was the rele-
vant threshold to trigger these procedural obligations. Bolivia maintained that notification and 
consultation were only required where there was a risk of a significant harm to the other party, 
whereas Chile argued that there was an obligation to provide information on planned meas-
ures, regardless of whether there was a risk of harm. Chile relied in part upon Article 11 of 
the 1997 Convention on the Law of the Non-Navigational Uses of International Watercourses 
(1997 Convention),107 which it suggested was a codification of customary international law. 
However, the Court rejected this argument, noting that the commentary of the International 
Law Commission (ILC) relating to Article 11 did not refer to any state practice or judicial 
authority to support the contention that it was a reflection of custom.108 The Court also consid-
ered the relevance of Article 12 of the 1997 Convention, which provides in part:
Before a watercourse State implements or permits the implementation of planned measures 
which may have a significant adverse effect upon other watercourse States, it shall provide 
those States with timely notification thereof.
Chile argued that this provision imposed a lower threshold than a risk of significant harm, rely-
ing upon the commentary of the ILC, which had expressly stated that the threshold of signifi-
cant adverse effect was lower than significant harm. The Commission had explained:109
“Significant harm” is not an appropriate standard for the setting in motion of the procedures 
under articles 12 to 19, since use of that standard would mean that the procedures would be 
engaged only where implementation of the new measures might result in a conduct covered 
by article 7 [on the prevention of significant harm]. Thus, a watercourse State providing a 
notification of planned measures would be put in the position of admitting that the measures 
it was planning might cause significant harm to other watercourse States in conduct covered 
by article 7. The standard of a “significant adverse effect” is employed to avoid such a situation.

However, the ILC itself seems to have accepted the higher threshold of significant harm in its 
later work on transboundary harm, which emphasises that the whole point of consultation is 
to achieve acceptable solutions on minimising the risk of significant harm.110 This is also the 
position reflected in the previous jurisprudence of the Court.111 In the case at hand, the Court 
confirmed this position, holding that ‘Article 12 of the 1997 Convention does not reflect a rule 
of customary international law relating to international watercourses that is more rigorous than 
the general obligation to notify and consult’112 and each state is only required to notify and 
consult other states under customary international law ‘with regard to any planned activity that 
poses a risk of significant harm to that State’.113 When it comes to applying this standard to the 
facts, Chile’s case failed because it has not demonstrated, nor alleged, any risk of harm linked to 
Bolivia’s planned measures.114
6.  CONCLUSION
Persistent diplomacy has led to a number of significant developments in the past twelve months in 
several important environmental treaty regimes. These hard-won gains have taken many years to 
achieve, but further efforts are still needed to implement and operationalise these new instruments 
in an effective and equitable manner, if positive results are to follow. What many of the instruments 
underline is the need for the whole of society to involve themselves in promoting transformational 
change that can benefit both people and planet. Yet, time is pressing. Urgent action is the watch-
word of many of the instruments. It follows that mechanisms are necessary to ensure that states 
actually deliver what they have promised. Bespoke monitoring mechanisms have been put in place 
in many global environmental regimes. For example, as noted above, 2023 will see the first round 
of the global stocktake of commitments under the Paris Agreement, with the expectation that ‘the 
outcome … shall inform Parties in updating and enhancing, in a nationally determined manner, 
their actions and support…’115 Similar arrangements are in place to oversee the GBF. The BBNJ 
Agreement also foresees the establishment of an Implementation and Compliance Committee to 
oversee implementation in a ‘facilitative, non-adversarial and non-punitive’ manner.116
The question is whether such mechanisms are sufficient. Other accountability mechanisms 
loom in the background. For example, the requested advisory opinion from the ICJ on climate 
change is expected to provide clarity on ‘the legal consequences under these obligations for 
States where they, by their acts and omissions, have caused significant harm to the climate sys-
tem and other parts of the environment’.117 The BBNJ Agreement also provides for compul-
sory litigation where states cannot settle their disputes by other means118 and the human rights 
regime has demonstrated that it can be invoked where progress cannot be achieved through 
other domestic or international fora. Moreover, as the HLABEM report makes clear, calls for 
more radical reform to the international legal system, including improved accountability mech-
anisms, are not going away.
